ECE 6612

Email transport and message security

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows an email crossing several TLS connections while an end-to-end protected message remains inside them.

Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) submits and relays mail. The sending server uses the recipient domain’s DNS mail-exchanger (MX) records to locate a destination. Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) gives a client mailbox access and synchronized state. Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) supports message retrieval for local access. Webmail puts an HTTP application in front of mail operations. These protocols serve different parts of the message’s journey.

STARTTLS upgrades an existing connection. An SMTP client sends EHLO, reads the server’s capabilities, requests STARTTLS, completes a TLS handshake on the same connection and port, then begins the protected SMTP exchange with a new EHLO. Implicit TLS runs the TLS handshake immediately after TCP connects, before mail commands. Common ports are SMTP relay 25, submission 587 with STARTTLS or 465 with implicit TLS, IMAP 143 with upgrade or 993 implicit, and POP3 110 with STLS upgrade or 995 implicit.

With opportunistic TLS, delivery may fall back to plaintext if TLS is unavailable. An active intermediary who strips an unprotected STARTTLS advertisement can trigger that allowed fallback. A sender that requires authenticated TLS instead stops or defers delivery when its required endpoint checks fail. The sender’s acceptance policy determines whether an unusable protected connection becomes a delivery failure or plaintext exposure.

Each TLS session ends at its two peers. A mail server decrypts the incoming connection to process the message and creates another connection for the next hop. Encrypting all links therefore places those servers inside the plaintext trust boundary. End-to-end message encryption instead protects the message before submission and lets intermediate servers relay the resulting encrypted object.

Hybrid message encryption uses a fresh symmetric content key K to protect message M, producing ciphertext C = Enc_K(M). It protects K for the recipient using the recipient’s authentic public key, producing a wrapped key E. The recipient’s private key recovers K, and K opens C. Real formats specify authenticated encryption, key wrapping and the exact protected fields. A sender’s private signing key can separately sign covered message data; the recipient verifies that signature with the sender’s authentic public signing key.

Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) traditionally uses user endorsements and local trust policy for public-key bindings. Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) uses a certificate infrastructure. Both require correct public-key distribution, private-key protection, revocation and usable recovery. Routing metadata and uncovered headers can remain visible. Endpoints that decrypt the object can read it, and content filtering must operate where the content is accessible.

Example

An organization encrypts each SMTP hop and stores ordinary mail on its servers. Those servers can process message content because they terminate TLS. If a sender encrypts the message object for the recipient before SMTP submission, the relays carry that object while still observing routing information, timing and size. Each claim follows the endpoint at which its encryption ends.

Sources and scope
  • C18 Email Security: SMTP/IMAP/POP3, STARTTLS, hop boundaries, PGP and S/MIME.
  • RFC 8314: email submission/access TLS and common implicit-TLS ports; RFC 3207: SMTP STARTTLS.
  • RFC 8551: S/MIME message specification; RFC 9580: OpenPGP.

Practice

1. An intermediary removes STARTTLS from an SMTP capability reply. Compare a sender permitting plaintext fallback with one requiring authenticated TLS before transmission.

Identify the connection each policy accepts before releasing mail content.

The opportunistic sender may continue in plaintext under its fallback policy, exposing that hop’s content. The sender requiring authenticated TLS stops or defers when acceptable TLS cannot be established, preserving confidentiality at an availability cost. Endpoint identity validation is part of the required TLS policy.

2. For an encrypted and signed message from Ada to Ben, identify which keys let Ben recover content and verify the sender, and which assumption connects those keys to people.

Separate the recipient’s encryption role from the sender’s signing role.

Ben uses his private decryption key to recover the content key, then that symmetric key to open the protected content. He uses Ada’s authentic public signing key to verify her signature over the covered data. Correct identity-to-public-key bindings, established through the chosen trust system, connect those cryptographic roles to Ada and Ben.
